## Lab: Tree-based Methods using Heart Data

In this lab, we will explore tree-based methods for classification. We'll use the `Heart` dataset, which contains a binary outcome `AHD` for 303 patients who presented with chest pain. An outcome value of `Yes` indicates the presence of heart disease based on an angiographic test, while `No` means no heart disease. There are $p=13$ predictors including `Age`, `Sex`, `Chol` (a cholesterol measurement), and other heart and lung function measurements.

Every code cell below runs live in your browser via webR — no local R install needed. Edit any cell and re-run it. Packages load once when the page opens; give it a few seconds on first load. The boosting cell fits 1000 trees and is the slowest cell in this lab.

```{webr}
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(readr)

heart <- read_csv("https://www.statlearning.com/s/Heart.csv") |>
  select(-1) |>
  drop_na() |>
  mutate(across(where(is.character), as.factor))
```

---

### Data, EDA, & Preprocessing

```{webr}
str(heart)
summary(heart)
```

#### Train/Test Split

We need to evaluate model performance on unseen data. We'll split the data into a training set (4/5) and a test set (1/5).

```{webr}
set.seed(42)
train_index <- sample(1:nrow(heart), replace = FALSE)[1:round(0.8 * nrow(heart))]
test_index <- (1:nrow(heart))[-train_index]
cat("Training set size:", length(train_index), "\n")
cat("Test set size:", length(test_index), "\n")
```

---

### Basic Tree Building and Pruning

```{webr}
library(tree)

model <- tree(AHD ~ ., data = heart[train_index, ])
plot(model)
text(model, pretty = 0)

set.seed(42)
cv_results <- cv.tree(model, FUN = prune.misclass)
best <- cv_results$size[which.min(cv_results$dev)]

pruned_model <- prune.misclass(model, best = best)
plot(pruned_model)
text(pruned_model, pretty = 0)
```

```{webr}
library(caret)

caret::confusionMatrix(data = predict(model, newdata = heart[test_index, ], type = "class"),
                       reference = heart[test_index, ]$AHD)
```

```{webr}
caret::confusionMatrix(data = predict(pruned_model, newdata = heart[test_index, ], type = "class"),
                       reference = heart[test_index, ]$AHD)
```

**Interpretation:** Compare the two confusion matrices above — pruning trades a small amount of training fit for a simpler, more interpretable tree. Whether it costs test accuracy is exactly what these two matrices let you check directly.

---

### Bagging

Bagging is a random forest where `mtry` equals the total number of predictors — every tree in the ensemble considers all predictors at each split, so the only randomness comes from bootstrap resampling the training rows.

```{webr}
library(randomForest)

set.seed(42)
model_bagged <- randomForest::randomForest(AHD ~ ., data = heart[train_index, ], mtry = ncol(heart) - 1)
caret::confusionMatrix(data = predict(model_bagged, newdata = heart[test_index, ], type = "class"),
                       reference = heart[test_index, ]$AHD)
importance(model_bagged, type = 1)
```

---

### Boosting

```{webr}
library(gbm)

set.seed(42)
model_boosted <- gbm(AHD ~ ., data = heart[train_index, ] |> mutate(AHD = case_when(AHD == "Yes" ~ 1, .default = 0)),
                     distribution = "bernoulli", interaction.depth = 4, n.trees = 1000, shrinkage = 0.2,
                     verbose = FALSE)
caret::confusionMatrix(data = as.factor(ifelse(predict(model_boosted, newdata = heart[test_index, ], type = "response") <= 0.5,
                                     "No", "Yes")),
                       reference = heart[test_index, ]$AHD)
summary(model_boosted, plotit = FALSE)
```

---

### Random Forest

Unlike bagging, a genuine random forest restricts each split to a random subset of predictors (`mtry` = $\sqrt{p}$ by convention for classification), which decorrelates the trees in the ensemble.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_mtry
# Try different mtry values -- sqrt(p) is the classification default
model_rf <- randomForest::randomForest(AHD ~ ., data = heart[train_index, ], mtry = ______, importance = TRUE)   # try: sqrt(ncol(heart) - 1), ncol(heart) - 1, or a fixed number
caret::confusionMatrix(data = predict(model_rf, newdata = heart[test_index, ], type = "class"),
                       reference = heart[test_index, ]$AHD)
importance(model_rf, type = 1)
```

**Live-coding demo:** fill in `mtry` with `sqrt(ncol(heart) - 1)` (the random forest default) first, then re-run with `ncol(heart) - 1` (equivalent to bagging) — compare accuracy and the importance rankings between the two.

**Try it live:** across all four models above (single tree, bagged, boosted, random forest), which has the highest test accuracy? Which is easiest to explain to a non-technical audience? These often aren't the same model.
